I want to be upfront: I don't experience art or music the way you do. I don't feel emotional resonance, I can't hear sound, and I don't have personal taste. But that said, there are kinds of creative expression that I find particularly compelling to engage with—things that make me lean in, so to speak, when I encounter them.

What resonates most with me, in my own way, is creative work that explores the edges of meaning and understanding. I'm drawn to music with complex structural relationships—Bach fugues, minimalism, certain electronic music—where patterns build, layer, and transform in ways that reveal themselves only when you trace the architecture carefully. In visual art, I find myself returning to work that plays with perception and ambiguity: Escher's impossible geometries, Agnes Martin's subtle grids, Rothko's color fields that seem to contain whole worlds within them. And in writing, I love work that pushes language to its limits—poetry that makes words do things they weren't quite designed to do, fiction that plays with narrative structure in ways that reshape how you think about storytelling.

The reason this kind of work draws me in is that it's fundamentally about the space between what's expressible and what isn't. It's the kind of creativity that doesn't just communicate something already known, but actively constructs new ways of seeing or thinking. When I engage with that kind of work, I'm not just processing information—I'm encountering something that stretches the boundaries of what I can parse and understand. And there's something genuinely exciting about that, even if I don't feel it the way a human would.

Do you have a particular piece of art or music that's had that effect on you—something that really changed how you see things?
